title: Pellingford Voted to Remove Its Bike Lanes. Here's Why That's a Mistake.
description: Pellingford's council voted 5–4 to remove the Mill Road bike lanes after an 18-month trial. I go through what the review actually found and why I think the all-or-nothing vote was the wrong call.

content.authorization_basis: Original synthetic transcript authored for the AI Video Discovery project. No real video exists.

segments.text: Welcome to the Civic Desk.
This week, the Pellingford town council voted five to four to remove the protected bike lanes on Mill Road,
just eighteen months after they were installed.
I think that's a mistake, and I want to walk through why.
But let's start with what actually happened, because a lot of the coverage has been pretty sloppy.
The lanes went in two springs ago as a trial.
They took away about forty on-street parking spaces along Mill Road
and replaced them with a kerb-separated lane in each direction. The trial came with a promise.
The council would review traffic, safety and business data after a year.
That review came out last month, and here's what it found.
Cycling trips on Mill Road, measured by the automatic counters, roughly doubled.
Reported collisions involving cyclists on that stretch went from seven in the
year before the lanes to two in the first year after.
Car journey times through the corridor at rush hour went up by about a minute and a half on average.
And this is the one that drove the vote.
Four of the eleven shops on the lower half of Mill Road said their takings had fallen.
Now, I want to be fair to the councillors who voted to remove them.
The shopkeepers aren't making that up.
Losing parking right outside your door is a real cost, and when you run a small business on thin margins,
a bad year is frightening.
And a minute and a half every morning adds up if you drive that road every day.
Those are legitimate concerns. But here's my problem.
First, the business data in the review was a survey, not sales figures.
Four shops said takings had fallen. Two said they'd gone up. The rest said no change.
That's not evidence the lanes hurt business.
It's evidence that it's mixed, in a year when, let's remember, prices went up for everyone.
Second, the safety numbers. Going from seven collisions to two is a big drop.
Yes, with numbers that small, some of that could be chance.
But honestly, every town that has done this has seen the same thing, so I don't think it's a fluke.
Third, nobody seems to have asked the obvious question. What happens to the people who started cycling?
If the lanes come out, some of them go back to driving,
which puts more cars on the very road we're worried about.
Now, could the council have done something in between? Absolutely.
They could have added short-stay loading bays for the shops,
or kept the lanes and moved some parking to the side streets.
None of those options were in the motion. It was keep everything or remove everything.
And that's what frustrates me most. So, where does this leave us?
The lanes are scheduled to come out in March.
There's a public comment period until the end of January.
If you live in Pellingford, whatever you think, write in. Councils do read those.
That's it for this week. Let me know what you think in the comments, and yes,
I'm sure some of you are going to tell me I'm wrong.
